Multimodal AI for Agentic System Failure Diagnosis and Root-Cause Reasoning

Jaydev Butani, Lavanay Mutreja, Mahit Turakhia, Het Shah
Under the Guidance of Prof. Aniket Shahade
Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, Symbiosis Institute of Technology (SIT), Pune, India
Project Repository: https://github.com/jaydevbutani/multimodal-agent-failure-diagnosis
Abstract

Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly entrusted with complex, multi-turn software development, shell navigation, and API orchestration. However, ensuring operational reliability remains fundamentally difficult: agents frequently succumb to silent, emergent behavioral pathologies such as cyclic retry thrashing, tool instability, sandbox environment permission denial, and unbounded information over-exploration. Existing observability solutions treat agents either as opaque black-box web services (monitoring solely latency and token cost) or rely on brittle post-hoc human inspection. In this work, we present a comprehensive, leakage-safe machine learning and forensic framework that reframes agent reliability through heterogeneous multi-view execution-trace fusion. We jointly model dense tabular execution telemetry (turn statistics, error frequencies, normalized code churn, duration, and information-theoretic tool entropy) alongside ordered discrete tool-call sequences.

Using the verified Agent Diagnostics benchmark comprising 11,995 execution trials across 61 software benchmarks and multiple frontier LLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Haiku, GPT-4o), we establish a strict grouped task-splitting protocol (task_id grouping) that guarantees zero cross-task data leakage across 8,298 training, 1,701 validation, and 1,996 unseen test trials. We systematically compare five model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, a sequential BiLSTM, and a proposed Cross-Modal Gated Multi-View Fusion Network. Evaluated on the 1,996 completely unseen test trials, experimental results demonstrate a critical operational trade-off: while XGBoost achieves the strongest balanced Macro-F1 ($0.7659$) and PR-AUC ($0.7132$), and Random Forest attains peak overall accuracy ($84.27\%$) and specificity ($91.7\%$), our proposed Multi-View Fusion Network achieves the highest Failure Recall ($72.95\%$), correctly catching 321 out of 440 true failure cases. This represents a $+15.0$ percentage-point absolute improvement and a $+25.9\%$ relative gain in detected failures over Random Forest. Furthermore, we decouple statistical failure prediction from diagnostic attribution, developing an evidence-based forensic engine that pinpoints suspicious turns, attributes component failures, and suggests actionable mitigations. Finally, we provide both a high-throughput Flask-based SVG Trace Canvas observability platform and a Streamlit research console, facilitating interactive diagnosis and live sandbox simulation.

Keywords: Autonomous AI Agents, Agent Observability, Failure Diagnosis, Multimodal Fusion, Telemetry Modeling, Root-Cause Analysis, Tool-Call Sequences, BiLSTM, XGBoost, Reliability Engineering.

1. Introduction

The paradigm of artificial intelligence has experienced a profound shift from passive language prediction to autonomous, interactive agency. Modern agentic architectures—such as OpenHands, SWE-Agent, Aider, and AutoGen—combine frontier foundation models (e.g., Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o) with external execution environments, allowing agents to inspect file trees, execute arbitrary bash commands, navigate web browsers, and author multi-file software patches. By iteratively executing ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) loops, these agents autonomously decompose overarching programming specifications into granular tool calls.

Despite impressive demonstrations, deploying autonomous agents in mission-critical environments introduces unprecedented software reliability risks. Unlike traditional deterministic software systems that fail with explicit stack traces, and unlike static machine learning models whose errors manifest as isolated misclassifications, agentic failures are emergent, sequential, and silent. An agent may execute 60 consecutive turns without triggering an uncaught Python exception, yet fail completely to accomplish the user task because it entered an infinite loop of executing identical grep commands, or thrashing repeatedly on a failing unit test without adapting its hypothesis.

Current industry observability tools (e.g., LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Datadog LLM Observability) predominantly monitor superficial API telemetry, including HTTP request latency, token consumption, and model invocation counts. While necessary for billing and latency monitoring, these metrics provide virtually zero insight into execution correctness or failure etiology. When an agent execution fails, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) and software teams are forced to manually parse transcripts spanning tens of thousands of tokens, searching for the decisive mistake step that derailed the trajectory.

To resolve this challenge, this research paper formulates automated agent failure detection and root-cause localization as a heterogeneous multi-view representation learning problem. An agent execution trial naturally contains two complementary representations:

  • Structured Execution Telemetry: Aggregated continuous and discrete counters, including total turns, tool execution error counts, retry frequencies, unique files read, lines of code modified (patch churn), cumulative execution duration, and information-theoretic diversity.
  • Ordered Action Trajectories: The temporal, discrete Markovian sequence of tool invocations ($ ext{read\_file} o ext{grep} o ext{str\_replace} o ext{execute\_bash}$) reflecting the agent's problem-solving strategy and behavioral transitions.

We demonstrate that fusing these complementary views provides superior sensitivity to system failure compared to analyzing either view in isolation. Crucially, we maintain strict scientific integrity by demonstrating that while tree-based ensembles (XGBoost) excel at balanced tabular discrimination, our proposed deep multi-view fusion architecture excels at failure sensitivity (recall), minimizing the catastrophic risk of silent, unflagged agent failures.

2. Background and Problem Context

To understand why autonomous agent failure diagnosis requires specialized machine learning architectures, one must examine the operational structure of an autonomous agent session. An agent operates within a discrete feedback loop formalized as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). At turn $t$, the agent receives an observation $o_t$ (terminal stdout, test logs, file contents), updates its internal working context, generates a reasoning trace, and emits an action $a_t$ corresponding to a tool invocation with structured arguments.

Because foundation models operate probabilistically, minor errors in environment feedback often trigger compounding failure cascades. Through systematic empirical analysis of verified execution benchmarks, we categorize agent failure modes into five canonical behavioral pathologies:

  1. Cyclic Retry Thrashing: The agent encounters an unexpected error (e.g., an unsatisfied module dependency or syntax error) and repeatedly executes the identical command or minor syntactic variations without altering the underlying environment state. This behavior is characterized by escalating turn latency and near-zero tool sequence entropy.
  2. Environment & Sandbox Crashes: The execution environment encounters catastrophic infrastructure failure, including Docker daemon socket disconnection, permission denial (HTTP 403 / EACCES), or out-of-memory container termination. Such failures manifest as high error frequencies during early initialization turns.
  3. High Code Churn Pathology: The agent repeatedly modifies source files, reverts edits, and introduces large, erratic diffs without satisfying target unit tests. This behavior is characterized by high patch-size-to-file ratios without task completion.
  4. Information Over-Exploration: The agent becomes trapped in exploratory code navigation, issuing dozens of find, grep, and cat commands without ever transitioning to active code repair or test execution.
  5. Tool Execution Instability: The agent invokes commands with invalid argument schemas, non-existent flags, or malformed JSON, causing tools to repeatedly return non-zero exit codes.

3. Literature Review

Research into LLM agent reliability and evaluation has accelerated rapidly across software engineering, systems engineering, and machine learning communities. We review prior work across three primary dimensions: agent benchmark frameworks, failure attribution methodologies, and trace representation learning.

Agent Evaluation Benchmarks: Early benchmarks such as AgentBench (Pan et al., 2024) and SWE-bench (Yang et al., 2024) pioneered rigorous, sandbox-verified evaluation of autonomous coding agents. SWE-bench established a gold standard by testing agents on thousands of real-world GitHub issues from major open-source Python repositories (e.g., SymPy, Django, scikit-learn). However, SWE-bench measures exclusively the binary end-to-end outcome: whether the generated patch passes unit tests. It provides zero intermediate telemetry or diagnostic guidance regarding why an agent failed.

Trajectory & Error Analysis: Addressing this limitation, recent work has explored intermediate trajectory inspection. Shinn et al. (2023) proposed Reflexion, which enables agents to reflect upon verbal feedback from failing trials; however, Reflexion relies on the LLM itself to identify errors, which frequently fails when the agent hallucinates or suffers from context saturation. Zhang et al. (2025) introduced Who&When (ICML 2025 Spotlight), presenting a hand-crafted and algorithmically generated benchmark for attributing failure to specific agents and steps in multi-agent workflows. Similarly, Jarmak (2025) released the Agent Diagnostics observatory, logging detailed turn-level telemetry, tool execution sequences, and verifier outcomes across thousands of coding trials.

Heterogeneous Trace Representation: In the systems observability domain, classical root-cause analysis has relied on either tabular metrics (CPU, memory, request error rates) via tree ensembles or distributed trace graphs via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). However, LLM agent execution traces differ fundamentally from microservices: agent actions are governed by language model semantics and structured tool schemas. Pure sequence models (BiLSTMs, Transformers) capture Markovian tool transitions but ignore continuous resource costs, while tabular gradient boosters capture cumulative churn but lose temporal ordering. Our research synthesizes these paradigms through multi-view representation learning.

4. Research Gap

A critical synthesis of the literature reveals three fundamental research gaps at the intersection of machine learning and autonomous systems observability:

  1. The End-to-End Outcome Fallacy: Prior research overwhelmingly measures final pass/fail outcomes against unit tests, treating the agent's intermediate trajectory as a black box. Consequently, when an agent fails after 40 turns, developers have no mechanism to determine whether failure stemmed from an early misconfiguration in Turn 3 or a late syntax error in Turn 38.
  2. Single-View Modality Insufficiency: Existing statistical failure detection attempts rely exclusively on static aggregated telemetry (ignoring action ordering) or sequence models (ignoring continuous physical duration, code churn, and error ratios). As demonstrated in our ablation experiments, neither view alone achieves optimal failure sensitivity.
  3. Conflation of Prediction and Causal Attribution: Several emerging observability tools conflate statistical failure prediction with causal root-cause reasoning. A machine learning model outputting $P( ext{failure}) = 0.92$ indicates high risk, but does not provide an actionable explanation of why the failure occurred or which component is responsible. Decoupling statistical prediction from deterministic evidence extraction remains unaddressed in the literature.

5. Problem Statement & Mathematical Formulation

Let an agent execution trial be represented as an ordered tuple:

$$\mathcal{T} = (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{m})$$ (1)

where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a continuous feature vector of $d=21$ execution telemetry metrics, $\mathbf{s} = (t_1, t_2, \dots, t_L)$ is an ordered discrete sequence of $L$ tool call tokens drawn from a finite vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ ($|\mathcal{V}| = 35$, truncated/padded to $L=50$), and $\mathbf{m}$ is a categorical tuple encoding metadata $( ext{model}, ext{agent\_name}, ext{benchmark})$.

Task 1: Out-of-Sample Binary Failure Classification. Learn a parameterized mapping $f_ heta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{m}) o [0, 1]$ estimating the posterior failure probability:

$$\hat{y} = P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{m})$$ (2)

where the true label $y \in \{0, 1\}$ is determined by sandbox test suite verification ($y=0$ if the patch passes all unit tests; $y=1$ if the agent crashes, times out, or fails verification). The binary classification decision is governed by a calibrated threshold $ au$:

$$\hat{C}_ au = \mathbb{I}(\hat{y} \ge au)$$ (3)

Task 2: Evidence-Based Turn Localization & Attribution. Given an execution trace flagged as failed ($\hat{C}_ au = 1$), determine the decisive failure step $k^* \in \{1, \dots, L\}$ and attribute the failure to a canonical behavioral signature $\mathcal{S} \in \{ ext{Thrashing}, ext{Crash}, ext{Churn}, ext{Exploration}, ext{Instability}\}$:

$$k^* = rg\max_{k \in \{1, \dots, L\}} \Phi( ext{turn}_k, \mathbf{x}_{1:k})$$ (4)

where $\Phi$ denotes an attribution scoring function incorporating turn latency, non-zero exit codes, and sequence entropy collapse.

6. Research Objectives

To resolve the stated problem statement with academic rigor, this project pursues five specific objectives:

  • Objective 1 (Dataset Ingestion & Leakage-Safe Partitioning): Ingest the verified 11,995-trial Agent Diagnostics dataset and implement a grouped task partitioning scheme based on task_id to strictly guarantee zero cross-task data leakage between training, validation, and test splits.
  • Objective 2 (Domain-Specific Feature Engineering): Formulate and validate 10 domain-specific derived telemetry features capturing normalized error rates, command retry ratios, search-to-edit quotients, code edit churn, and Shannon tool sequence entropy.
  • Objective 3 (Multimodal Architecture Design): Design, implement, and train a dual-stream deep neural network featuring an MLP tabular encoder, a Bidirectional LSTM trajectory encoder, and a learnable cross-modal gating fusion mechanism.
  • Objective 4 (Rigorous Benchmark & Trade-Off Analysis): Benchmark the proposed fusion network against four competitive baselines (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and sequence-only BiLSTM) across seven standard evaluation metrics, analyzing operational trade-offs between precision, accuracy, and failure recall.
  • Objective 5 (Diagnostic Platform Implementation): Develop an interactive, production-grade observability platform featuring an SVG Execution DAG Trace Canvas, temporal telemetry charts, and an AI Forensic Assistant providing decoupled, evidence-based failure attribution.

7. Proposed System Overview

The proposed framework operates as an asynchronous, non-invasive observability sidecar that hooks into agent runtime environments. During execution, our instrumentation collects step-level tool dispatches, file system diffs, and execution latencies without interfering with model reasoning. Upon session termination (or dynamically at intermediate checkpoints), the trace payload is ingested by our processing pipeline.

The pipeline decomposes the payload into two parallel representations: continuous scalar telemetry and an integer-encoded tool transition sequence. The tabular stream is standardized and projected into a 64-dimensional latent embedding through dense layers with batch normalization. Concurrently, the sequence stream passes through an embedding layer and a bidirectional recurrent network, with temporal max-pooling capturing critical transition bottlenecks. A learnable gating network dynamically calculates the relative contribution of telemetry versus trajectory context, emitting a calibrated failure probability. Finally, if failure risk exceeds the calibrated threshold ($ au = 0.46$), the trace is routed to our forensic rule engine, which extracts concrete execution evidence, localizes the suspicious step, and outputs structured remediations.

8. Dataset Description and Provenance

To ensure absolute empirical honesty, we explicitly document the origin, licensing, and characteristics of the datasets utilized in this research.

8.1 Primary Supervised Dataset: Agent Diagnostics Observatory

The primary dataset is the Agent Diagnostics repository authored by S. Jarmak (2025), released under the open-source Apache License 2.0. The raw dataset artifact resides locally at data/raw/agent_diagnostics/signals.parquet (file size: 1.48 MB; SHA-256 integrity hash: 4cea2359787900e8fc20e0e583b21763da99f46d99868cf7f18a1877c9425222).

The dataset contains 11,995 verified execution trials generated by autonomous software engineering agents across 61 distinct software engineering benchmarks (including openhands, sdlc_fix, sdlc_feature, org_migration, and org_security). The trials encompass multiple frontier LLM backends: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, claude-sonnet-4-6-20251001, claude-opus-4-6-20251001, and gpt-4o-2024-08-06.

Each trial record consists of 32 original fields, encompassing:

  • Identification & Metadata: trial_id, task_id, model, agent_name, config_name, benchmark.
  • Quantitative Telemetry: total_turns, tool_calls_total, search_tool_calls, edit_tool_calls, code_nav_tool_calls, semantic_search_tool_calls, unique_files_read, unique_files_edited, error_count, retry_count, patch_size_lines, duration_seconds.
  • Categorical Exception Flags: rate_limited (boolean), exception_crashed (boolean).
  • Tool Call Trajectory: tool_call_sequence (ordered Python list of tool identifiers invoked during the session).
  • Ground-Truth Outcome: passed (boolean) and continuous reward ($[0.0, 1.0]$). We define the failure indicator as $y = eg ext{passed}$.
Figure 2. Empirical dataset characteristics: (Left) Overall class distribution across 11,995 verified trials showing a 3.34:1 class imbalance ratio; (Right) Sample counts across training, validation, and test splits following strict grouped task partitioning with zero task overlap.

8.2 Missing Value Audit & Data Hygiene

An audit of signals.parquet indicates that numerical telemetry fields exhibit 0% missing values. Certain sequence lists (e.g., files_read_list, files_edited_list) contain empty arrays for trials where the agent crashed before executing file operations; these are handled cleanly as empty string representations. Missing target values do not exist, as all 11,995 trials completed sandbox test evaluation.

8.3 Secondary Temporal Benchmark: Who&When

To evaluate turn-level localization beyond tabular metrics, we incorporate the Who&When benchmark (Zhang et al., ICML 2025 Spotlight; MIT License) residing at data/raw/who_when/. This benchmark contains 184 full multi-agent trajectories (4,092 execution turns) across GAIA and AssistantBench. We utilize Who&When specifically to validate our forensic turn-attribution logic against dual-annotated human ground truth.

9. Data Preprocessing & Leakage Prevention

A critical vulnerability in published agent research is data leakage across identical tasks. In coding benchmarks, multiple trials solve the identical task problem using different model configurations. If trials sharing the same task_id are randomly assigned across train and test sets, models memorize task-specific repository idiosyncrasies, inflating test accuracy by 10–18 percentage points.

9.1 Grouped Task Partitioning

To enforce strict out-of-sample evaluation, we implement Grouped Shuffle Splitting grouped by task_id using sklearn.model_selection.GroupShuffleSplit (seed $= 42$). The complete dataset of 11,995 records is partitioned as:

  • Training Partition: **8,298 trials** ($69.2\%$), encompassing 845 unique software tasks, with a failure rate of $22.95\%$.
  • Validation Partition: **1,701 trials** ($14.2\%$), encompassing 172 unique software tasks, with a failure rate of $23.16\%$. Used for hyperparameter tuning and decision threshold calibration.
  • Test Partition: **1,996 trials** ($16.6\%$), encompassing 869 unique software tasks, with a failure rate of $22.04\%$. Held out strictly for final evaluation.

We explicitly verify that the task intersections between splits are empty:

$$\mathcal{T}_{ ext{Train}} \cap \mathcal{T}_{ ext{Val}} = \emptyset, \quad \mathcal{T}_{ ext{Train}} \cap \mathcal{T}_{ ext{Test}} = \emptyset, \quad \mathcal{T}_{ ext{Val}} \cap \mathcal{T}_{ ext{Test}} = \emptyset$$ (5)

guaranteeing that test set performance reflects genuine generalization to unseen software engineering problems.

9.2 Training-Only Transformer Fitting

To eliminate data leakage, all scalers and encoders are fitted strictly on the 8,298 training trials:

  • Numerical Scaling: Continuous features are normalized using StandardScaler: $$z = rac{x - \mu_{ ext{train}}}{\sigma_{ ext{train}}}$$
  • Categorical Encoding: Categorical metadata (model, agent_name, benchmark) is encoded using OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False), producing 67 binary columns. Unseen categories in test sets map to zero vectors.
  • Skew Stabilization: Features exhibiting extreme right-skewness (execution duration, patch size) are stabilized via $\ln(1 + x)$ transformations prior to standardization.

10. Domain-Specific Feature Engineering

Raw counters alone fail to capture operational dynamics. For example, an agent performing 20 tool calls with 4 errors has an error rate of $20\%$, whereas an agent with 4 tool calls and 4 errors has an error rate of $100\%$. We formulate 10 domain-specific derived features computed strictly from intra-session telemetry (zero target leakage):

Table 2: Formulations and Rationales for the 10 Domain-Specific Derived Features
Feature Name Mathematical Definition Domain Interpretation Diagnostic Value
DERIVED_error_rate $ rac{ ext{error\_count}}{\max(1, ext{tool\_calls\_total})}$ Tool failure density per invocation Flags fragile sandbox environments
DERIVED_retry_ratio $ rac{ ext{retry\_count}}{\max(1, ext{error\_count})}$ Quotient of errors triggering retries Detects cyclic thrashing loops
DERIVED_search_to_edit_ratio $ rac{ ext{search\_tool\_calls}}{\max(1, ext{edit\_tool\_calls})}$ Exploration vs. exploitation balance Identifies over-exploration loops
DERIVED_edit_churn $ rac{ ext{patch\_size\_lines}}{\max(1, ext{unique\_files\_edited})}$ Average lines modified per edited file Detects erratic patch generation
DERIVED_tool_intensity $ rac{ ext{tool\_calls\_total}}{\max(1, ext{total\_turns})}$ Tool density per conversational turn Identifies parallel tool execution
DERIVED_read_to_edit_ratio $ rac{ ext{unique\_files\_read}}{\max(1, ext{unique\_files\_edited})}$ Information intake vs. code mutation Separates read thrashing from edits
DERIVED_time_per_turn $ rac{ ext{duration\_seconds}}{\max(1, ext{total\_turns})}$ Average wall-clock latency per turn Flags command hangs & timeouts
DERIVED_tool_entropy $-\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} p_t \ln p_t$ Shannon entropy over tool sequence Low entropy indicates cyclic loops
DERIVED_log_duration $\ln(1 + ext{duration\_seconds})$ Log-stabilized session latency Normalizes heavy right-skew
DERIVED_log_patch_size $\ln(1 + ext{patch\_size\_lines})$ Log-stabilized modified patch lines Prevents outlier gradient explosion

11. Machine Learning Methodology

To rigorously assess the utility of multi-view fusion, we construct a hierarchy of five machine learning models representing distinct inductive biases:

11.1 Classical Tabular Baselines

1. Logistic Regression (Baseline): Serves as our linear separability baseline, trained using $L_2$ regularization (penalty weight $C=1.0$, solver=lbfgs) over the 88-dimensional transformed feature vector.

2. Random Forest (Balanced): A bagging ensemble of 200 decision trees (max_depth=15, min_samples_split=5) trained with class_weight='balanced' to mitigate the 3.34:1 class imbalance. Random Forest captures complex non-linear feature interactions without gradient instability.

3. XGBoost Classifier: A gradient boosted decision tree ensemble (n_estimators=250, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=6, subsample=0.8, scale_pos_weight=3.34). XGBoost represents the gold standard for structured tabular telemetry.

11.2 Sequence Trajectory Model (BiLSTM)

To evaluate whether tool transitions alone predict failure, we implement a pure sequence model ignoring tabular telemetry. Tool tokens are mapped to a 32-dimensional embedding space:

$$\mathbf{E} = ext{Embedding}(\mathbf{s}) \in \mathbb{R}^{L imes 32}$$ (6)

The sequence is processed by a 2-layer Bidirectional LSTM:

$$\mathbf{h}_t = [\overrightarrow{ ext{LSTM}}(\mathbf{E}_t) \,;\, \overleftarrow{ ext{LSTM}}(\mathbf{E}_t)] \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$$ (7)

Temporal max-pooling extracts the most salient transition features across time: $\mathbf{h}_{ ext{pooled}} = \max_{t} \mathbf{h}_t$, followed by a linear classification head.

12. Proposed Cross-Modal Gated Multi-View Fusion Network

The core contribution of this work is the Cross-Modal Gated Multi-View Fusion Network (Figure 3), designed to dynamically weight continuous telemetry against discrete trajectory patterns.

Figure 3. Detailed architecture of the proposed Cross-Modal Gated Multi-View Fusion Network, showing dual-stream encoding, the learnable gating mechanism, and the binary failure prediction head.

Tabular Encoder: The 88-dimensional tabular input $\mathbf{x}_{ ext{tab}}$ passes through a multi-layer perceptron with Batch Normalization and Dropout:

$$\mathbf{h}_{ ext{tab}} = ext{ReLU}\left(\mathbf{W}_2 \cdot ext{Dropout}\left( ext{ReLU}\left( ext{BN}\left(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x}_{ ext{tab}} + \mathbf{b}_1 ight) ight) ight) + \mathbf{b}_2 ight)$$ (8)

where $\mathbf{W}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{128 imes 88}$, $\mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{64 imes 128}$, producing embedding $\mathbf{h}_{ ext{tab}} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$.

Trajectory Sequence Encoder: Concurrently, tool sequence $\mathbf{s}$ is mapped via embedding and a Bidirectional LSTM ($d_{ ext{hidden}} = 32$), followed by temporal max-pooling and projection:

$$\mathbf{h}_{ ext{seq}} = ext{ReLU}\left(\mathbf{W}_{ ext{proj}} \left(\max_{t \in [1, L]} \mathbf{h}_t^{ ext{BiLSTM}} ight) + \mathbf{b}_{ ext{proj}} ight) \in \mathbb{R}^{64}$$ (9)

Learnable Gating Fusion Mechanism: Rather than simple concatenation or static averaging, we implement a parameterized gating function $lpha \in [0, 1]^{64}$ that dynamically calculates whether telemetry or trajectory provides the stronger predictive signal for the given trial:

$$lpha = \sigma\left(\mathbf{W}_g [\mathbf{h}_{ ext{tab}} \,;\, \mathbf{h}_{ ext{seq}}] + \mathbf{b}_g ight)$$ (10)
$$\mathbf{h}_{ ext{fused}} = lpha \odot \mathbf{h}_{ ext{tab}} + (1 - lpha) \odot \mathbf{h}_{ ext{seq}}$$ (11)

where $\mathbf{W}_g \in \mathbb{R}^{64 imes 128}$, $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function, and $\odot$ represents the Hadamard element-wise product.

Classification Objective: The fused embedding passes through a dense layer emitting logit $z$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{ ext{BCE}} = - rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ w_1 y_i \log \sigma(z_i) + w_0 (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \sigma(z_i)) ight]$$ (12)

optimized using AdamW ($ ext{learning\_rate} = 10^{-3}$, $ ext{weight\_decay} = 10^{-4}$) with early stopping on validation loss.

13. Experimental Results & Evaluation

All models were evaluated on the 1,996 unseen test trials (Class 0: 1,556, Class 1: 440) using predictions saved in data/processed/test_predictions.parquet. To account for the 3.34:1 class imbalance, decision thresholds were calibrated on the validation set, identifying $ au = 0.46$ as the optimal operating point.

14. Comparative Analysis & Operational Trade-Offs

An honest scientific analysis requires rejecting false claims of universal superiority. The experimental results reveal nuanced trade-offs dictated by model architecture:

  1. XGBoost for Balanced Classification: XGBoost achieves the highest Macro-F1 ($0.7659$) and Precision-Recall AUC ($0.7132$). Its gradient-boosted decision trees effectively carve the orthogonal feature thresholds characteristic of resource telemetry (e.g., error rate $\ge 0.15$ combined with retry ratio $\ge 0.10$).
  2. Random Forest for Specificity & Accuracy: Random Forest achieves peak Accuracy ($84.27\%$), ROC-AUC ($0.8632$), and Precision ($66.41\%$), exhibiting high specificity ($91.7\%$). However, it is conservative: it achieves only $57.95\%$ failure recall, missing 185 out of 440 actual failures.
  3. Multi-View Fusion for High-Stakes Reliability (Peak Recall): In production Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), false negatives (silent unflagged agent failures) carry vastly higher operational cost than false positives (which merely trigger human inspection). The proposed Multi-View Fusion Network attains the highest Failure Recall ($72.95\%$), catching 321 out of 440 failures and reducing missed failures to 119.
    • Absolute Improvement: $+15.0$ percentage points over Random Forest ($72.95\% - 57.95\%$).
    • Relative Improvement: $+25.9\%$ relative increase in detected failures ($ rac{0.7295 - 0.5795}{0.5795}$).
Figure 5. Dissected confusion matrices for Random Forest, XGBoost, and the Proposed Multi-View Fusion Network across 1,996 test trials, illustrating the reduction in False Negatives (FN) from 185 to 119 in the Fusion Network.
Figure 6. Discrimination curves on 1,996 unseen test trials: (Left) Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves; (Right) Precision-Recall (PR) curves relative to class prevalence baseline ($0.220$).

15. Modality Ablation Study

To verify whether multi-view fusion provides genuine empirical gain over single modalities, we conduct an ablation isolating each view:

Table 4: Modality Ablation Analysis (1,996 Unseen Test Trials)
Configuration / Modality Tested Input Representation Failure Recall (%) PR-AUC (%) Macro-F1 (%)
View 1 Only: Sequence Trajectory Tool Sequence BiLSTM 67.27% 59.36% 72.93%
View 2 Only: Structured Telemetry Tabular XGBoost 67.05% 71.32% 76.59%
Multi-View Fusion: Telemetry + Sequence Dual-Stream Gated Network 72.95% 69.49% 74.86%
Figure 7. Modality ablation comparison demonstrating that fusing tool trajectories with continuous telemetry yields the highest Failure Recall ($72.95\%$), confirming that temporal sequencing disambiguates high-risk telemetry.

16. Interpretability & Feature Attribution Analysis

To prevent the system from operating as an uninterpretable black box, we perform feature importance and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) attribution on the tabular telemetry features.

Figure 8. Feature interpretability analysis: (Left) Information gain ranking of the top 15 predictive features; (Right) SHAP summary beeswarm plot illustrating feature impact on failure likelihood.

The interpretability results confirm strong domain intuitions:

  • DERIVED_edit_churn & patch_size_lines: Rank as the strongest predictive signals. In software agents, massive diffs across numerous files strongly correlate with hallucinated code generation and regression failures.
  • DERIVED_tool_intensity & total_turns: High turn counts with low tool intensity indicate stalling and reasoning loops.
  • DERIVED_tool_entropy: Shannon entropy below $0.5$ strongly drives positive SHAP values toward failure, verifying that repetitive retry loops are a reliable indicator of task derailment.

Important Methodological Caveat: We emphasize that high SHAP attribution denotes predictive association, not mathematical causality. Telemetry features reflect behavioral symptoms of underlying model cognitive breakdown.

17. Forensic Root-Cause Diagnostic Reasoning Framework

A core tenet of this research is the deliberate decoupling of statistical failure prediction from evidence-based diagnostic reasoning. While deep neural networks excel at estimating $P( ext{failure})$, neural attention weights cannot reliably pinpoint causal software bugs.

Our system implements a secondary rule-driven forensic attribution pipeline (Figure 9) that interrogates execution artifacts once a trial is flagged as high-risk ($\hat{y} \ge 0.46$).

Figure 9. Decoupled two-stage diagnosis pipeline: Stage 1 performs neural multi-view failure prediction; Stage 2 performs deterministic evidence extraction, signature classification, and turn-level fault localization.
Table 5: Diagnostic Attribution Signatures, Heuristics, and Actionable Remediation Actions
Failure Signature Trigger Telemetry Conditions Execution Trace Evidence Recommended SRE Remediation
Cyclic Retry Thrashing retry_ratio > 0.15 & tool_entropy < 0.60 $\ge 3$ consecutive executions of identical bash/tool commands Inject loop-break interrupt; force alternative tool strategy or request human guidance.
Environment Crash error_count $\ge 5$ within first 10 turns Permission denial (EACCES), missing docker socket, missing dependencies Verify container image base; inspect volume mount permissions and network egress.
High Code Churn edit_churn > 80 lines/file & unique_files_edited > 4 Repeated full-file rewrites without passing intermediate test suites Revert working directory to baseline commit; constrain edit scope to localized symbols.
Over-Exploration Loop search_to_edit_ratio > 4.0 & edit_tool_calls == 0 $\ge 12$ consecutive find, grep, or read_file dispatches Inject semantic file map or symbol table into context to focus search window.
Tool Instability Non-zero exit codes on diverse tools ($> 3$ distinct tools) Malformed JSON arguments, invalid CLI flags, unescaped strings Validate tool JSON schemas; enable strict structured outputs on foundation model.

18. Interactive Observability Platform & User Interface

To translate this research into practical engineering utility, we developed a production-ready web application running on Flask and Jinja2 (available at http://127.0.0.1:8502), alongside a companion Streamlit research console (app/main.py).

Figure 10. Production Agent Trace Canvas interface showing: (Top) 7-Card interactive scenario selection grid; (Center) Bounded execution DAG with dynamic Bézier curves, status rings, and isolated zoom/fit controls; (Right) Docked node parameter inspector; (Bottom) Temporal step latency area curves with failure pin attribution and forensic reasoning recommendations.

18.1 Key Application Capabilities

  1. Interactive Execution DAG (Trace Canvas): Renders agent execution turns as a bounded Directed Acyclic Graph. Nodes feature status-colored rings (green for success, crimson pulse for errors), step numbers, tool icons, and execution latency badges. Viewport transformations (Zoom In, Zoom Out, Fit) are isolated from the sidebar inspector.
  2. 7-Card Scenario Selection Grid: Enables instant, one-click evaluation of real benchmark traces (Nominal Run, Retry Thrashing, Environment Crash, High Churn, Over-Exploration, Tool Instability, Compound Failure).
  3. Multi-Model Diagnostic Selector: Allows users to dynamically toggle inference between the Proposed Fusion Network, XGBoost, Random Forest, BiLSTM, and Logistic Regression, observing probability shifts in real-time.
  4. Temporal Step Latency Curve: Area chart displaying execution duration per turn with a red pin marker pinpointing the suspicious failure turn ($k^*$).
  5. AI Forensic Assistant: Outputs structured natural-language diagnostics explaining what happened, what went wrong, and actionable SRE remedies.
  6. Persistent Diagnostic History & Deep-Linking: Saves evaluated sessions to an SQLite database, supporting deep-linking (/trace-canvas?history_id=...) to restore exact historical trace DAGs without fallback.

19. Empirical Case Study: Real-World Agent Failure Localization

To illustrate end-to-end diagnosis, we examine a real failure trace from the benchmark: 02_retry_thrashing (Task: task_retry_loop_bash, Model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001).

Trace Execution Profile: The agent was tasked with resolving a dependency conflict. In Turn 1, it read package.json (latency: 18ms). In Turn 2, it executed npm test (failed with Exit Code 1: Cannot find module 'lodash'). In Turns 3 through 12, the agent entered an unconstrained retry loop, re-executing npm test and npm install without administrative permissions.

Diagnostic Output:

  • Model Probability: Proposed Multi-View Fusion Network predicts $P( ext{failure}) = \mathbf{0.9514}$ (Status: FAILURE DETECTED, Risk: High).
  • Signal Telemetry: 12 total tool calls, 9 errors ($75.0\%$ error rate), 9 retries (retry quotient: $1.0$), tool entropy: $0.693$ (severe collapse).
  • Localized Failure Step: Step 04 — execute_bash.
  • Root-Cause Reasoning: Classified as Cyclic Tool Retry Thrashing. Forensic Assistant generates: "The agent entered a repeated tool-execution loop without making meaningful progress. 9 consecutive command retries were logged on execute_bash without addressing the root module error."
  • Actionable Remediation: "Force sub-goal re-evaluation; inject dependency cache or verify container npm registry access."

20. Discussion

The empirical findings of this project provide critical implications for the design of reliable autonomous agent systems:

The Value of Multi-View Fusion: Our ablation results prove that combining continuous telemetry with discrete action sequences provides superior failure recall ($72.95\%$) compared to analyzing either view in isolation. Tool sequences capture transition structure (e.g., repeated bash attempts), while continuous telemetry provides scale (e.g., whether the retry spanned 2 seconds or 500 seconds). Fusing both views resolves ambiguities that mislead single-view models.

Operational Model Selection in AgentOps: The trade-off between XGBoost and Multi-View Fusion highlights that model selection must align with operational priorities. In scenarios where human reviewer bandwidth is severely constrained and false alarms must be minimized, XGBoost represents the optimal choice (Macro-F1: $0.7659$). Conversely, in safety-critical automated harnesses where an undetected failure may corrupt production databases or deploy buggy code, the Multi-View Fusion Network's superior recall ($72.95\%$) makes it the strongly preferred architecture.

21. Limitations & Threats to Validity

In accordance with academic standards, we explicitly report five limitations of this study:

  1. Domain Concentration: The dataset focuses primarily on software engineering coding agents (OpenHands, SWE-bench). While the telemetry schema generalizes to shell and API tools, domain adaptation is required for embodied robotics or multimodal vision agents.
  2. Fixed Sequence Length Truncation: The BiLSTM branch truncates tool sequences to $L=50$. While $94\%$ of benchmark trials complete within 50 tool calls, ultra-long multi-turn sessions ($>200$ turns) require hierarchical recurrence or state-space models.
  3. Correlation vs. Causality: Telemetry indicators (e.g., high churn, error counts) represent statistical correlates of failure rather than formal mathematical proofs of causality.
  4. Post-Hoc vs. Real-Time Intervention: Our current implementation evaluates completed traces or historical checkpoints. Transitioning from post-hoc diagnosis to real-time, turn-by-turn early termination requires online prefix-sequence calibration.
  5. Dataset Model Diversity: While the dataset spans Claude-3.5 and GPT-4o, open-weight reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) exhibit distinct reasoning patterns that warrant future evaluation.

22. Ethical & Practical Considerations

Deploying automated failure diagnosis systems introduces both safety benefits and ethical responsibilities. By detecting silent agent thrashing, our system directly prevents runaway cloud compute costs and denial-of-service loops on third-party APIs. Furthermore, automated failure attribution promotes algorithmic accountability by clearly distinguishing whether a task failure was caused by model cognitive failure, prompt ambiguity, or external sandbox infrastructure crashes.

All datasets analyzed in this research were published under permissive open-source licenses (Apache 2.0, MIT). The traces do not contain private personal identifiable information (PII), proprietary source code, or unredacted authentication tokens.

23. Future Work

We identify four promising trajectories for extending this research:

  • State-Space Trajectory Modeling: Replacing the BiLSTM sequence encoder with selective state-space architectures (Mamba) to support unbounded turn trajectories without quadratic memory complexity.
  • Active Circuit-Breakers: Integrating the failure prediction model as an online circuit-breaker directly inside agent frameworks (e.g., LangChain, AutoGen) to pause execution and prompt human intervention before token budgets are exhausted.
  • Causal Counterfactual Diagnosis: Incorporating Structural Causal Models (SCMs) to test whether modifying a specific tool output in Turn $k$ would have counterfactually prevented task failure.
  • Multi-Agent Graph Neural Networks: Expanding the trajectory model to heterogeneous graph neural networks (GNNs) capturing inter-agent message passing and responsibility delegation.

24. Conclusion

As autonomous AI agents transition from experimental curiosities to critical software infrastructure, automated observability and failure diagnosis become imperative. In this research, we presented a comprehensive, leakage-safe machine learning framework for agent failure detection and root-cause reasoning. By fusing dense structured telemetry with sequential tool action trajectories across 11,995 verified trials, our proposed Cross-Modal Gated Multi-View Fusion Network achieves a peak Failure Recall of $72.95\%$ on unseen software tasks—a $+15.0$ percentage-point improvement over balanced Random Forest. By decoupling statistical prediction from evidence-based forensic localization, our architecture provides actionable diagnostic transparency. The open-source platform, interactive Trace Canvas, and reproducible code provide a robust foundation for future research in autonomous AI reliability engineering.

A.2 Step-by-Step Pipeline Execution Instructions

# 1. Clone the official project repository
git clone https://github.com/jaydevbutani/multimodal-agent-failure-diagnosis.git
cd multimodal-agent-failure-diagnosis

# 2. Initialize and activate virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate  # On Linux: source .venv/bin/activate

# 3. Install verified dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

python src/preprocessing/prepare_data.py

python src/models/classical_models.py

# 6. Train deep trajectory and multimodal fusion architectures
python src/models/deep_models.py

# 7. Run full test evaluation and calculate exact out-of-sample metrics
python src/evaluation/verify_predictions.py

# 8. Launch the Flask Interactive Trace Canvas Observability Platform
python run.py
